entries.ipa: /əˈlɔŋ wɪð/ (also /əˈlɑŋ/ with the cot–caught merger; with also /wɪθ/) · weak /əˈlɔŋ wəð/, /əˈlɔŋ wəθ/
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause, never a bare or to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] along with [noun phrase] / [subject], along with [noun phrase], [singular verb] / Along with [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with together with, which is the more written of the two. Neither can do the instrumental work of plain with — you cut bread with a knife, not along with one. And along with is a preposition, not and: it does not make a singular subject plural.
entries.meaning: Joins a second party or a second item to what has already been named, either as company on the way or as one more thing in the pile. It is the everyday additive of American speech and writing, equally at home in a shipping manifest and in conversation. 1. In the company of. Two people or things moving or acting together. 2. In addition to. One more item added to a list, a price, or a transaction. 3. Appended to a subject. The verb still agrees with the original subject alone.
examples: She rode out to the site along with two state inspectors.
The dog came along with us on every trip that summer.
The sale includes the appliances along with all the patio furniture.
Bring a photo ID along with a copy of the lease.
The governor, along with three of her aides, was subpoenaed.
Interest, along with late fees, is added to the balance every month.

entries.ipa: full /æz ˈwɛl æz/ · weak /əz ˈwɛl əz/ — both instances of as reduce, and the weak form is what you actually hear
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund; a bare infinitive when the main verb is itself a bare or to-infinitive (She can act as well as sing) — never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] as well as [noun phrase] / [subject], as well as [noun phrase], [singular verb] / [verb-ing] … as well as [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: As well as is not and. And builds a compound subject and takes a plural verb; as well as subordinates the second item, so the verb agrees with the first subject alone — The pitcher, as well as two relievers, was ejected. Keep it apart from the comparative adverbial as well as meaning "as skillfully as" (He plays as well as she does), which is a different construction with a clause after it.
entries.meaning: Adds a second item while keeping the first one in the foreground. This asymmetry is the whole point of the word: A and B gives the two equal billing, A as well as B makes B the afterthought — which is exactly why the verb never notices it. 1. In addition to a noun. 2. Linking two verbs. The second verb goes to -ing, unless a modal or a to-infinitive already governs it. 3. Appended to a subject. Singular subject, singular verb.
examples: The clinic treats adults as well as children.
She speaks Portuguese as well as Spanish.
He runs the front desk as well as handling the schedule.
The grant covers tuition as well as paying for books.
She wanted to direct as well as act.
The mayor, as well as two council members, was invited.
Fuel, as well as labor, accounts for most of the increase.

entries.register: neutral; a fixture of advertising, real-estate copy, and description
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — no gerund, no finite clause, no infinitive.
entries.pattern: [noun] complete with [noun phrase] / [clause], complete with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Complete with is not including. Including names a member of a set that has already been counted; complete with presents the extra as equipment the whole thing arrives furnished with. It is also positionally restricted where including is not: it postmodifies a noun or trails a clause and cannot open a sentence — ✗ Complete with a canoe, the cabin rents by the week. Against together with, which merely adds, complete with implies the addition finishes the picture, and that implication is what makes it the standard vehicle for a dry joke.
entries.meaning: Presents a thing along with everything that outfits it. It sells hard, and because it sells so hard, half its working life is spent being sarcastic. 1. Listing what comes with a thing. 2. In descriptions of costume, staging, and setting. 3. Sarcastically, for an unwelcome extra.
examples: The cabin rents complete with linens, firewood, and a canoe.
They delivered the grill complete with a cover and a full tank of propane.
He showed up in a three-piece suit, complete with pocket watch.
The lobby has been restored complete with the original brass mailboxes.
We got the whole presentation, complete with the slideshow.
It was a classic family dinner, complete with an argument about the will.

entries.register: neutral to formal; the analyst's and the reporter's word
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], coupled with [noun phrase], [verb agreeing with the first noun] / Coupled with [noun phrase], [clause] / coupled with [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Where along with and together with merely add a second item, coupled with claims the two work on each other to produce the result the main clause names. It is the causal member of the additive family, and swapping it for and loses that claim. Its agreement behavior is the family rule: Drought, coupled with two failed harvests, was enough to empty the valley — singular, because coupled with is a preposition and not a conjunction.
variants: combined with, paired with, allied to — the same construction under different metaphors
entries.meaning: Joins two factors and reports what they do together. Reporters and analysts reach for it whenever one cause alone would be too simple an explanation. 1. Naming two factors behind one result. 2. Adding a condition to an obligation or an offer. 3. With a gerund. 4. Appended to a subject. The verb agrees with the original subject alone.
examples: Low inventory, coupled with cheap credit, pushed prices past any honest appraisal.
Coupled with the new tariffs, the shipping delays wiped out the quarter.
The grant carries a five-year commitment coupled with an annual audit.
A guilty plea coupled with full restitution usually keeps a first offender out of prison.
Coupled with having to retrain the whole staff, the software change cost them a season.
The rent increase, coupled with losing two tenants, put the building underwater.
Fatigue, coupled with poor visibility, was listed as the probable cause.
The deductible, coupled with the monthly premium, makes the policy a bad deal.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — the to here is a preposition, so a bare infinitive is an error: in addition to working, never in addition to work full time. No finite clause.
entries.pattern: In addition to [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] in addition to [noun phrase] / in addition to [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: The to-trap it shares with look forward to, object to, and be used to: the to is a preposition and demands -ing. Against as well as, it is heavier and more likely to open a sentence; against besides, it is unambiguous — besides can also mean "except for", and in addition to never can.
entries.meaning: Names something extra that stands alongside what the main clause says, with no suggestion that either item is the more important. Because it is transparently compositional, it survives in formal writing where plus and besides would sound casual. 1. Adding a noun. 2. Adding an activity — always -ing. 3. Appended to a subject. The verb agrees with the subject alone.
examples: In addition to the fine, he lost his license for ninety days.
The apartment comes with a parking space in addition to a storage locker.
In addition to working full time, she takes two night classes.
In addition to running the shop, he does all the bookkeeping himself.
The principal, in addition to four teachers, was placed on leave.
In addition to the tuition, students pay a lab fee and a parking permit.

entries.type: marginal/participial (fully grammaticalized — it needs no subject to control it)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a wh-clause (including how the money was spent, including whether the lease can be broken) — one of the very few prepositions in this file that takes one. Never a that-clause and never a tensed clause on its own: ✗ including it was raining.
entries.pattern: [total set], including [member], … / [amount] including [component] / including but not limited to [list]
entries.contrast: The mirror of excluding. Against inclusive of, which is a commercial and contractual word attaching to a noun, including attaches loosely to a whole clause and is unrestricted in register. Against postposed included (tax included), which follows its noun rather than preceding it. Note that including names a sample, not the whole list — which is why American drafters write including without limitation when they need to say so out loud.
entries.meaning: Picks out one or more members of a set that has just been named, or folds a component into a total. It does not claim the list that follows is complete, and in careful writing it should not be used as if it were: if the set really is exhausted, write namely or consisting of. 1. Naming members of a set. A pronoun after it goes in the objective case — including me, never including I. 2. Counting something into a total. 3. The drafting formula. Used when the list must be read as open-ended. 4. Before a wh-clause. The complement is a question folded into a noun slot. 5. With a gerund.
examples: Nine passengers, including the pilot, walked away from the crash.
Several states, including Ohio and Nevada, have already certified.
Everyone including me had to retake the certification.
The rate is $180 a night, including breakfast.
That comes to $42 including tax and delivery.
All benefits, including but not limited to health and dental coverage, continue through June.
The tenant pays all utilities, including without limitation gas, electric, water, and trash.
The audit covers everything, including how the reserve fund was spent.
Several questions remain, including whether the lease can be broken at all.
The job has its costs, including driving ninety minutes each way.
She listed her objections, including having to sign a five-year lease.

entries.ipa: /ɪnˈklusɪv ʌv/ · weak /ɪnˈklusɪv əv/, reduced /ɪnˈklusɪvə/ before a consonant
entries.register: formal; chiefly commercial, contractual, and hospitality writing
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause.
entries.pattern: [noun] inclusive of [noun phrase] / [price] is inclusive of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The exact opposite of exclusive of, and the stiff twin of including. Including can float anywhere in a sentence; inclusive of almost always postmodifies a noun or follows the verb be. Do not confuse the preposition with the adjective inclusive in a date range (March 3 through March 9 inclusive), which takes no of — and which American English rarely needs, since through is already inclusive where British to is not.
entries.meaning: Declares what a stated price, figure, or period already contains. It exists because contracts and invoices need a word that cannot be misread, and it buys that precision at the cost of sounding like a contract. 1. Of a price, a rate, or a fee. The commonest use by far. 2. Of a figure, a headcount, or a package. 3. Of a span of dates. Where American English usually says through instead.
examples: All quoted prices are inclusive of shipping and handling.
Rent is $2,150 a month, inclusive of water, sewer, and trash.
The flat fee is inclusive of all filing costs.
Salaries are stated inclusive of the employer's retirement contribution.
The package is inclusive of airfare, transfers, and two guided excursions.
Headcount stands at 240, inclusive of contractors and seasonal staff.
The blackout period runs March 3 to March 9, inclusive of both dates.
Coverage is inclusive of the first and the last day of the term.

entries.ipa: /lɛt əˈloʊn/ · reduced /lɛɾ əˈloʊn/ — the t flaps between vowels
entries.type: marginal (a frozen imperative that has become a connective)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, adjective, adverb, prepositional phrase, gerund, or a bare infinitive matched to the verb before it (can't walk, let alone run) — never a finite clause, and never a to-infinitive when the verb before it is bare: ✗ can't walk, let alone to run. Requires a negative, near-negative, or question earlier in the sentence — not, never, nobody, nothing, hardly, barely, too … to, can't. Without one it is ungrammatical: ✗ He can drive, let alone fly a plane.
entries.pattern: [negative clause], let alone [phrase parallel to what preceded] / can't [bare verb], let alone [bare verb] / not [noun], let alone [noun]
entries.contrast: Let alone is the mirror image of not to mention and to say nothing of. All three add a second item at the end, but not to mention upgrades — what follows is the heavier item actually in play — while let alone downgrades: what follows is the more extreme thing that is even further out of reach. He can't drive, let alone fly a plane says flying is the harder claim; reverse the two and the sentence collapses. Note also that whatever follows must be parallel to what preceded it: a bare verb answers a bare verb, a noun answers a noun.
variants: much less — fully interchangeable in American English; never mind (informal) and still less (formal) do the same work.
entries.meaning: Adds a second item only to say that it lies even further beyond whatever was just denied. It is a scaling device rather than a true addition: the first item marks the floor and let alone points past it. 1. After a negative, before a noun phrase. 2. Before a bare infinitive matched to the verb before it. 3. Before an adjective, an adverb, or a prepositional phrase. 4. In questions and after near-negatives.
examples: There wasn't enough money for repairs, let alone a new roof.
He doesn't have a driver's license, let alone a car.
She can't walk to the mailbox, let alone run a 10K.
Most of them couldn't find the building, let alone get past the front desk.
The road isn't paved, let alone plowed.
Nobody goes down there in daylight, let alone after dark.
Who has time for lunch, let alone a two-hour meeting?
The team barely made the playoffs, let alone a deep run.

entries.ipa: /ˌnɑt tə ˈmɛnʃən/ · reduced /ˌnɑʔ tə ˈmɛnʃən/ — the t of not glottalizes and to is always the weak /tə/, never /tu/
entries.type: marginal (a frozen infinitival that has become a preposition)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, adjective, or a wh-clause. A that-clause only through the fact that (not to mention the fact that nobody asked). Never a bare finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause], not to mention [noun phrase] / [adjective], not to mention [adjective] / [clause], not to mention [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Against in addition to and as well as, which are neutral, not to mention is rhetorical: it pretends to omit the item while naming it, so whatever follows is always the heavier or the more damning of the two. It is also positionally fixed — it comes at the end of what it adds to and never opens a sentence: ✗ Not to mention the cost, the plan is impractical; write The plan is impractical, not to mention ruinously expensive.
variants: to say nothing of — a shade more formal and fully interchangeable. Distinguish let alone, which reverses the polarity: it needs a negative before it and downgrades what follows (He can't drive, let alone fly a plane), where not to mention upgrades.
entries.meaning: Adds one last item under the pretense of skipping it. The pretense is the whole device: what follows lands harder than what came before precisely because the speaker claimed not to be bringing it up. 1. Adding a heavier item at the end of a list. 2. Adding an adjective. A construction almost no other preposition allows. 3. With a gerund. 4. With the fact that, where a clause is unavoidable.
examples: The repair took three weeks and two thousand dollars, not to mention a rental car.
She runs the department and teaches two seminars, not to mention a research group of nine.
The apartment is tiny, not to mention four flights up.
The plan is expensive, not to mention flatly illegal.
He had to redo three years of taxes, not to mention explaining the whole thing to his brother.
Moving in February means ice and a truck deposit, not to mention taking a week off work.
The lease is a bad deal, not to mention the fact that the building is for sale.
He missed three deadlines, not to mention the fact that nobody could reach him for a week.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ˈtɑp ʌv/ · weak /ɑn ˈtɑp əv/, reduced /ɑnˈtɑpə/ before a consonant — the of loses its /v/ exactly as it does in out of
entries.register: neutral; the additive sense is conversational and nearly always aggrieved
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (on top of paying rent); a nominal wh-clause is possible in the additive sense (on top of what the movers charged). Never a that-clause and never a to-infinitive: ✗ on top of pay rent. Bare on top is an adverb and takes no object — the berries go on top — and that is the test: the preposition must have something after it.
entries.pattern: On top of [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] on top of [noun phrase] / on top of [verb-ing] / on top of everything else
entries.contrast: The literal sense — the keys are on top of the refrigerator — is a spatial preposition and is covered with the complex prepositions; what belongs in this file is the additive one. Against in addition to, which is neutral and formal, on top of is informal and carries a complaint built in: the second item is a burden piled on the first, which is why on top of the rent is idiomatic and on top of the bonus sounds odd. Against besides, it can never be read as "except for". A third idiom, on top of meaning "in full control of" (she's on top of every deadline), is a separate sense again.
entries.meaning: Piles one more demand onto a load that was already heavy. It is the American complaint word of the additive family, and the only one that presupposes the addition is unwelcome. 1. In addition to — with the second item as a burden. 2. With a gerund. 3. The fixed phrase on top of everything else. 4. Before a wh-clause.
examples: On top of the rent, they pay their own utilities and trash.
The clinic charges a facility fee on top of the doctor's bill.
On top of working two jobs, she's finishing a degree at night.
On top of having to repaint, we found rot under the siding.
On top of everything else, the furnace quit on the coldest night of the year.
She lost the contract and, on top of that, the client wants the deposit back.
On top of what the movers charged, we paid two weeks of storage.
On top of whatever the insurer covers, there's a $2,000 deductible.

entries.ipa: /ˌoʊvər ənd əˈbʌv/ · weak /ˌoʊvɚ ən əˈbʌv/ — the and is always reduced to /ən/ or /n̩/
entries.register: formal to neutral; standard in compensation, contracts, and budgets
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; a gerund is possible but uncommon (over and above having to repay the advance). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [amount] over and above [amount] / [clause] over and above [noun phrase] / Over and above [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Over and above is in addition to with one extra claim built in: the addition sits on top of a baseline that has already been satisfied. A bonus over and above base salary means the salary was already paid in full; an hour over and above the minimum means the minimum was already met. Where in addition to is neutral about the first item, over and above certifies it. Do not read the phrase compositionally — it is frozen, and neither over nor above keeps its spatial meaning inside it.
entries.meaning: Names what is added once an obligation has already been discharged. It is the standard phrase for a bonus, an overage, and a duty gone beyond. 1. Money added to an amount already owed. 2. Effort or service beyond a required minimum. 3. Adding a further consideration to an argument.
examples: The bonus is paid over and above base salary.
Any expenses over and above the retainer must be approved in writing.
She did that work over and above anything the job actually required.
The district demands sixty hours of training over and above the state minimum.
Over and above the cost, there's the question of whether anyone would use it.
The building is unsafe, and over and above that, it isn't even zoned for offices.

entries.register: neutral as a preposition; the sentence-initial Plus, is informal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; a gerund is possible but rare (plus having to repaint). Never a finite clause. The word is also an adjective (a plus sign, an A plus), a noun (that's a real plus), and an informal sentence adverb (Plus, it's cheaper) — in those uses it has no object and is not a preposition.
entries.pattern: [number] plus [number] / [amount] plus [noun phrase] / Plus, [clause] (adverb — informal)
entries.contrast: Plus is not and. And makes a compound subject and takes a plural verb; plus is a preposition, so The base salary plus the bonus was more than he expected keeps the singular. In arithmetic, Two plus two is four is the standard form. Against minus, its arithmetic opposite; against in addition to, its formal equivalent — a job application should not begin a sentence with Plus.
entries.meaning: Adds one quantity or item to another. It began life as the Latin word for "more" in arithmetic and spread outward from there into prices, packages, and finally into casual speech as a discourse connector. 1. Arithmetic addition. 2. With the addition of. A cost, a component, an extra. 3. And also. An extra item, slightly informal. 4. As a sentence adverb — not a preposition. No object follows; informal.
examples: Six plus four is ten.
The perimeter is the length plus the width, doubled.
Rent is $1,400 a month plus utilities.
At closing you'll owe the principal plus accrued interest.
He brought his cousin plus two friends nobody had met.
She got the promotion plus a corner office.
It's too far to drive. Plus, the parking is impossible.
The seats are terrible, and plus they cost twice as much.

entries.ipa: /tə ˈseɪ ˈnʌθɪŋ ʌv/ · weak /tə ˈseɪ ˈnʌθɪŋ əv/, reduced /tə ˈseɪ ˈnʌθɪŋə/ before a consonant — the to is always the weak /tə/, never /tu/
entries.type: complex (a frozen infinitival that has become a preposition)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or adjective; a that-clause only through the fact that. Never a bare finite clause, and — because the of is a preposition — never a bare infinitive: to say nothing of paying for it, not ✗ to say nothing of pay for it.
entries.pattern: [clause], to say nothing of [noun phrase] / [clause], to say nothing of [verb-ing] / [adjective], to say nothing of [adjective]
entries.contrast: The formal twin of not to mention; the difference is register, not sense. To say nothing of is what you meet in edited prose, not to mention is what you hear. Both are rhetorical rather than neutral — whatever follows is the heavier item, named under the pretense of being skipped — and both are positionally fixed at the end of what they add to: ✗ To say nothing of the cost, the plan is impractical. Against let alone, which reverses the polarity and downgrades what follows, to say nothing of always upgrades.
variants: not to mention — the spoken equivalent, and interchangeable in almost every context
entries.meaning: Names one more item while claiming to pass over it. Like not to mention, the pretense is the whole device, and register is the only thing that separates the two. 1. Adding a heavier item at the end of a list. 2. With a gerund. 3. Adding an adjective or a further judgment. 4. With the fact that, where a clause is unavoidable.
examples: The delay cost them the season, to say nothing of the money.
Two of the exhibits were mislabeled, to say nothing of the one that never arrived.
He'd have to sell the house, to say nothing of explaining it to his sister.
Rewriting the code took a month, to say nothing of testing it.
The proposal is expensive, to say nothing of legally doubtful.
The trip was long and cold, to say nothing of pointless.
The deal is bad on its face, to say nothing of the fact that nobody on the board has read it.
She was unqualified, to say nothing of the fact that she had been fired twice.

entries.register: formal to neutral; standard in legal and conveyancing language
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] together with [noun phrase] / [subject], together with [noun phrase], [singular verb]
entries.contrast: The formal twin of along with, and the two are freely interchangeable in meaning. Neither is instrumental — that is plain with. Like every word in this section, it is a preposition and does not pluralize a singular subject.
entries.meaning: Attaches a second item to the first in writing that wants to sound deliberate. It is the standard formula in deeds and contracts, where together with all appurtenances has been boilerplate for centuries, and it carries a trace of that formality into ordinary prose. 1. Accompanying an item in a transaction or a submission. 2. Adding one factor to another. 3. Appended to a subject. Singular verb.
examples: The deed conveys the parcel together with all easements and rights of way.
Please return the signed form together with a check for the filing fee.
Heat, together with the humidity, makes the afternoons unbearable.
Send the transcript together with three letters of recommendation.
The chairman, together with two board members, was named in the suit.
The principal, together with any unpaid interest, becomes due on demand.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a wh-clause (apart from what the neighbors told us, apart from whether it's legal) — never a that-clause and never a tensed clause on its own.
entries.pattern: Apart from [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] apart from [noun phrase] / apart from [verb-ing] / apart from [wh-clause]
entries.contrast: Apart from and aside from mean the same thing; aside from is the more American of the two and apart from the more British, though both are current in the United States. Both are ambiguous between "except for" and "in addition to", and only context settles it: after a plain positive claim they subtract, but before also, too, or as well, or alongside a negative, they add.
entries.meaning: Sets an item outside the claim being made — either by exempting it from a generalization or, in the additive reading, by putting it beside one. The literal reading, "at a distance from", is still live and is the source of both. 1. Except for. Subtracting a qualification. 2. In addition to. Adding one more item, usually signaled by also or a negative. 3. Before a wh-clause. 4. Separate from. The literal spatial sense, and the source of the other three.
examples: Apart from a scratch on the bumper, the car is in perfect shape.
Everyone apart from the two interns had already gone home.
Apart from being the cheapest option, it's also the fastest.
Apart from the tuition, there are lab fees and a parking permit.
Apart from what the neighbors told us, we know nothing about the family.
Apart from whether the roof will hold, there's the wiring to think about.
He stood apart from the rest of the group, saying nothing.
Keep the recyclables apart from the regular trash.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a wh-clause (aside from what it costs, aside from whether it's legal) — never a that-clause and never a tensed clause on its own.
entries.pattern: Aside from [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] aside from [noun phrase] / aside from [verb-ing] / aside from [wh-clause]
entries.contrast: Identical in meaning to apart from; the difference is geography, not sense. American writers reach for aside from first, British writers for apart from. Like apart from, it swings between subtraction and addition on the polarity of the sentence around it. Against except for, it is looser — except for commits to subtraction, aside from does not.
entries.meaning: The default American way to fence off an exception before making a general claim. It opens sentences more comfortably than almost anything else in this file, which is why it turns up constantly in reviews, summaries, and complaints. 1. Except for. 2. In addition to. 3. Before a wh-clause. 4. Opening a concession before the main point.
examples: Aside from a few typos, the draft is ready to send.
Nobody aside from the two of us knows the combination.
Aside from running the shop, he coaches a Little League team.
Aside from being illegal, it's a terrible idea.
Aside from whether it's legal, it's a terrible way to treat people.
Aside from what the inspector wrote down, nobody has said a word to us.
Aside from the cost, there's the question of whether it will even fit.
Aside from one bad winter, we've never had trouble with the pipes.

entries.register: formal and chiefly British in free use; standard in American English only inside the fixed phrase bar none
entries.complement: noun phrase — no gerund, no clause.
entries.pattern: [superlative claim], bar none / all bar [number] (chiefly British) / bar [noun phrase] (chiefly British)
entries.contrast: In American English bar survives almost entirely in bar none, a fixed tag meaning "with no exceptions at all" that follows a superlative. Where a British writer uses bar freely, an American writes barring or except for. Do not confuse the preposition with the verb bar (barred from the premises) or the several nouns.
entries.meaning: Built on the verb bar exactly as barring is, and now nearly frozen. In its one thriving American use it does no grammatical work beyond intensifying a superlative that has already been made. 1. The fixed American phrase. After a superlative: with no exceptions. 2. General exception — chiefly British. An American ear hears this as an import. 3. Not a preposition — the verb and the noun. The preposition takes an object and means "except"; the verb means "to shut out" and takes a direct object of its own, and the nouns are unrelated to both.
examples: It's the best barbecue in the state, bar none.
She is the finest trial lawyer in this building, bar none.
Every seat was sold, bar a handful in the last row.
All the runners finished bar one, who pulled up at mile eighteen.
Bar a late collapse, they'll take the division. (an American would write barring)
The court barred him from the property for a year. (verb)
They met at a bar two blocks from the courthouse. (noun)

entries.register: neutral; a staple of forecasting and sports and business journalism
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause. Not barring it rains; write barring rain or switch to the conjunction unless.
entries.pattern: Barring [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] barring [noun phrase] / barring [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Barring names a future contingency that would spoil an otherwise confident prediction; except for subtracts a real member from a set that already exists. Barring an injury looks forward, except for the injury looks back. Against failing, which is its near mirror: barring X frames X as the unwelcome disruption, failing X frames X as the outcome you were hoping for.
entries.meaning: Fences off the one thing that could go wrong and then makes the prediction anyway. It is the single most useful hedge in American reporting, because it lets a writer commit to a forecast while naming its escape hatch. 1. Excluding a contingency from a prediction. 2. Plain exception. Slightly formal, less common than sense 1. 3. With a gerund, and with an object plus a gerund.
examples: Barring a late snowstorm, the roads should be clear by Friday.
Barring injuries, this is the deepest roster they've had in years.
Barring something unforeseen, closing is set for the fifteenth.
Every member voted yes, barring two who abstained.
The archive is complete, barring a handful of volumes lost in the fire.
Barring getting called in, I'm free all weekend.
Barring the river coming up again, the crews will be finished by Thursday.

entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause.
entries.pattern: Bating [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause], bating [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: An archaic cousin of excepting and saving, formed from the verb abate, "to take away". No living American writes it; you meet it only in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century prose, where it means "leaving out of account". Modern equivalents: excepting, apart from, leaving aside. Do not confuse it with baiting (luring), and note that the bated of with bated breath is the same root but a frozen idiom, not this preposition.
entries.meaning: Sets a small deduction aside before endorsing the whole. It is included here for readers of older books, not as a word to use. 1. Setting a small deduction aside from a record or an agreement. 2. Excepting one person or one trait from a judgment.
examples: Bating a few small errors of transcription, the manuscript is faithful to the original.
The account is complete, bating the two pages torn from the ledger.
The terms were agreed, bating the question of the boundary line.
Bating his temper, he was as fine a foreman as the yard ever had.
All the company came away satisfied, bating one gentleman who had lost his hat.

entries.register: neutral; the adverb use is conversational
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause. A what-phrase after it (besides what he told us) is a fused relative, which is a noun phrase and not a clause; the test is that a plain noun can replace it (besides his statement). As an adverb it takes no object at all (Besides, it's too late), and that is its commonest use in speech.
entries.pattern: Besides [noun phrase], [clause] / [negative or question] besides [noun phrase] / besides [verb-ing] / Besides, [clause] (adverb)
entries.contrast: Beside vs. besides. Beside without the -s means "at the side of" and belongs with the position prepositions, along with the two frozen idioms beside the point and beside himself. Besides with the -s means "in addition to" or "except for", and is also an adverb meaning "anyway". Sit beside me / Nobody besides me came. Writing besides the point, or beside the salary there's a bonus, is a real and frequent error. Against except for and in addition to, besides is the ambiguous one — careful writers pick the unambiguous word when the reading matters.
entries.meaning: Puts one more item next to what has been said, or — after a negative — carves one out. It is the oldest of the additive prepositions and the only one that has also become a discourse marker, which is now what most Americans use it for. 1. In addition to. 2. Except for. Nearly always after a negative or an all-inclusive word. 3. With a gerund. 4. As an adverb — not a preposition. No object; means "anyway" or "moreover".
examples: Besides the mortgage, they're carrying two car loans.
Who else is coming besides your brother?
No one besides the surgeon was allowed in the room.
There's nothing in the refrigerator besides condiments.
Besides teaching, she edits a quarterly journal.
Besides costing twice as much, the new system is slower.
It's too far, and besides, I don't have the money.
I'm not going. Besides, I wasn't invited.

entries.type: simple; the same form is the coordinating conjunction but (see the conjunctions dictionary) and an adverb in all but
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun (objective case in American usage), an adverb or prepositional phrase (anywhere but here, any time but now), a bare infinitive after a do-phrase or after cannot (nothing to do but wait, one cannot but admire it), or a to-infinitive after choice, option, or alternative (no choice but to resign). The two infinitives are not interchangeable: ✗ nothing to do but to wait, ✗ no choice but resign. Never a finite clause — but that is the conjunction, not this preposition, and but never takes a gerund. Requires an all-inclusive or negative word earlier in the sentence — all, every, everyone, everything, everywhere, no one, nothing, nowhere, any-, a superlative, or a wh- question word. Without one it is ungrammatical: not I saw the movie but the ending, but I saw everything but the ending.
entries.pattern: [universal/negative word] but [noun phrase] / nothing but [noun phrase] / nothing to do but [bare infinitive] / no choice but to [verb] / cannot but [bare infinitive]
entries.contrast: Prepositional but is the tightly restricted twin of except, and where except can stand at the head of a sentence with for, but cannot — there is no ✗ but for the noise in this sense (but for is a separate, counterfactual preposition). Against the conjunction but, which joins two clauses of equal rank and reduces to /bət/: the preposition takes an object and is usually stressed. Case note: American usage takes the objective pronoun — everyone but me, no one but him. The traditional rule that a subject-position but-phrase takes the nominative (No one but he knew) is now bookish; No one but him knew is what educated Americans write and say.
entries.meaning: Subtracts one member from a set that has already been declared total. Because it depends entirely on that earlier totalizing word, it feels less like a preposition and more like a second half of a construction — which is why it also lives inside a handful of frozen quantifying phrases. 1. Except, after a universal or a negative. 2. Before an adverb or a prepositional phrase. 3. Before an infinitive — bare after a do-phrase, to after choice. This is the one place learners of English go wrong with but, and the two patterns do not mix. 4. In frozen quantifying phrases. Nothing but = only; all but = almost; cannot but = cannot help. 5. Not a preposition — the conjunction and the adverb. The preposition takes an object; the conjunction joins two units of equal rank and takes none, and the adverbial but means "only".
examples: Everyone but Marcus signed the petition.
The store is open every day but Sunday.
Nobody but you would have noticed.
He'd go anywhere but back to that office.
Any weekend but this one would work.
There was nothing to do but wait for the tow truck.
There is nothing left to say but congratulations.
They had no choice but to postpone the wedding.
With the bridge closed there was no option but to double back.
The season was nothing but injuries and rain delays.
The bill is all but dead in committee.
One cannot but admire the nerve of it. (formal)
I called twice, but nobody picked up. (conjunction — two clauses, no object)
The paint is dry but still tacky in one corner. (conjunction — two adjectives)
The tank was but half full when they set out. (adverb, "only" — formal and dated)

entries.ipa: /ˈbʌt fɔr/ · weak /ˈbʌt fɚ/ (also written /fər/), and in rapid speech /ˈbʌʔ fɚ/ with a glottal t
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — never a clause. To take a clause, write but for the fact that. Requires a counterfactual main clause, with would, would have, might have, or could have.
entries.pattern: But for [noun phrase], [subject] would (have) [verb] / [subject] would (have) [verb] but for [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: But for is not except for. Except for subtracts a real item from a real situation (Except for the dessert, the meal was excellent); but for deletes an item and reports what would have followed (But for the dessert, the meal would have been forgettable). Without says the same thing more plainly, and the everyday American equivalent is if not for, which requires exactly the same counterfactual main clause. It is unrelated to prepositional but.
entries.meaning: Names the one thing that stood between the world as it is and the world it would otherwise have been. Its home is American tort law, where but-for causation — the injury would not have occurred but for the defendant's conduct — is the standard test, and it carries that argumentative weight into ordinary prose. 1. Naming the decisive cause of a good outcome. 2. Naming the decisive obstacle to one. 3. In legal and financial argument.
examples: But for your testimony, the case would have been dismissed.
She would have drowned but for the lifeguard on the north jetty.
But for a flat tire, we'd have been there by noon.
But for the pandemic, the restaurant might still be open.
The company would be insolvent but for the parent's guarantee.
But for the officer's failure to secure the scene, the evidence would have been admissible.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, prepositional phrase (except in emergencies), adverb (except here, except yesterday), bare infinitive after do (nothing to do except wait), or to-infinitive (no choice except to agree). A finite clause is possible only through a following conjunction — except that, except when, except if, except where — and at that point except is a conjunction, not this preposition. Requires an all-inclusive word already in the sentence — all, every, everyone, everything, everywhere, always, nothing, no one, the whole. Without one, use except for.
entries.pattern: [totalizing word] except [noun phrase] / [clause] except [adverbial] / nothing to do except [bare infinitive] / except that [clause] (conjunction)
entries.contrast: Except vs. except for vs. excepting. Use except when a totalizing word is already present (everyone, all, nothing, every day). Use except for when there is no such word, when the phrase opens the sentence, or when the thing subtracted is not the same kind of thing as the set — Except for a few typos, the essay is clean, because typos are not essays. Excepting is formal and now confined to not excepting and always excepting. Sentence-initial bare except — Except the noise, it's fine — is an error. The test for the conjunction is the one used everywhere else in this file: the preposition takes an object, while except that, except when, and except if take a whole finite clause. And do not confuse any of it with the verb accept, which is a different word entirely.
entries.meaning: The plain, unmarked word for taking one member out of a stated whole. Everything else in this section is a stylistic or grammatical variation on it. 1. Subtracting a member from a total set. 2. Before an adverbial — a time, a place, a condition. 3. Before an infinitive. 4. Before a clause — with that, or in informal speech without it. Here it is a conjunction.
examples: Everyone except the two of us went home early.
She remembered nothing except the sound of the brakes.
The museum is open daily except Monday.
The rule applies everywhere except on federal land.
There was nothing to do except apologize and start over.
He had no option except to resign.
I'd have told you except that it wasn't mine to tell.
I'd go, except I'm broke until Friday. (informal)

entries.ipa: /ɪkˈsɛpt fɔr/ · weak /əkˈsɛpt fɚ/ (also written /fər/), and before a consonant often /əkˈsɛp fɚ/
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: Except for [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] except for [noun phrase] / except for [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Where except needs a totalizing word already in place, except for supplies its own frame and can open a sentence on its own. Except for is also the right choice when the thing subtracted is a different kind of thing from the set — a typo is not an essay, a squeak is not a car. Against but for, which is counterfactual and demands a would-clause; against apart from and aside from, which are looser and may be read additively.
entries.meaning: Withdraws a qualification from a claim that would otherwise be sweeping. It is the workhorse of the exception family in American English and the safe default when you are unsure whether bare except will hold. 1. Subtracting a flaw from a general endorsement. 2. Naming the only thing left in an otherwise empty scene. 3. Opening a sentence, where bare except cannot.
examples: Except for a cracked screen, the phone works fine.
The team played well except for the third quarter.
The house is empty except for a folding chair in the kitchen.
The lot was dark except for one security light over the door.
Except for Tuesdays, my afternoons are open.
Except for having to change planes in Dallas, it was an easy trip.

entries.complement: noun phrase — no gerund, no clause.
entries.pattern: not excepting [noun phrase] / always excepting [noun phrase] / [clause], excepting [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Excepting is what except for replaced. Outside the two fixed emphatics not excepting ("including even") and always excepting ("with the standing exception of"), it sounds stiff or antique in American prose. Excluding is the current neutral participial; saving and bating are the archaic ones.
entries.meaning: Marks an exemption with more ceremony than the situation usually requires. Its two surviving phrases pull in opposite directions: not excepting insists that nothing is exempt, always excepting insists that one thing permanently is. 1. Not excepting — including even. 2. Always excepting — with a standing carve-out. 3. Plain participial exception. Dated in American writing.
examples: All employees, not excepting senior partners, must complete the training.
The delegates voted unanimously, not excepting the two who had objected in committee.
The policy covers every kind of loss, always excepting acts of war.
The fee schedule applies to all filings, always excepting emergency petitions.
Every parcel on the block, excepting the corner lot, was rezoned.
All charges were dropped, excepting the count of criminal trespass.

entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in pricing, statistics, and specifications
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [total] excluding [noun phrase] / [clause], excluding [noun phrase] / excluding [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: The exact mirror of including, and the modern neutral replacement for excepting. Against except for, it is colder and more quantitative — excluding belongs on an invoice, except for belongs in a sentence. Exclusive of is its formal-contractual variant, not counting its conversational one. Against less and minus, which perform a real arithmetic subtraction: excluding only declares something out of scope.
entries.meaning: Draws a line around a figure or a set and says what is outside it. Because it is neutral and precise, it is the safe word wherever a number has to be defended. 1. Removing a component from a price. 2. Removing a group from a statistic. 3. Removing a member from a set.
examples: The list price is $34,900, excluding destination charges and tax.
The estimate covers labor only, excluding hauling away the old unit.
Enrollment rose four percent, excluding transfer students.
Revenue grew nine percent excluding currency effects.
Everyone on the roster, excluding the two on injured reserve, made the trip.
The building sleeps twelve, excluding the finished basement.

entries.ipa: /ɪkˈsklusɪv ʌv/ · weak /əkˈsklusɪv əv/, reduced /əkˈsklusɪvə/ before a consonant
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause.
entries.pattern: [noun] exclusive of [noun phrase] / [price] is exclusive of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The exact opposite of inclusive of, and the contractual twin of excluding. In ordinary American writing, not including or plus tax does the same work without the starch. Do not confuse it with the adjective exclusive meaning "restricted" or "sole" (an exclusive contract), which is a different sense of the same word.
entries.meaning: States what a quoted figure leaves out, in language a court could read. It is the price-list word, and it postmodifies a noun or follows be rather than floating freely through a sentence. 1. Of a price, a rate, or a fee. 2. Of a measurement or a headcount. 3. Of a span of dates.
examples: All prices are quoted exclusive of sales tax.
The rent is $1,900 a month, exclusive of utilities.
The retainer is exclusive of court costs and expert witness fees.
The trailer measures forty feet, exclusive of the tongue.
Headcount stands at 212, exclusive of contractors and seasonal staff.
The bid covers materials only, exclusive of the general contractor's fee.
The policy runs from the first of the month, exclusive of the day of purchase.
The notice period is fourteen days, exclusive of weekends and federal holidays.

entries.complement: noun phrase — most often the pronouns that and which (failing that, failing which), and otherwise an abstract noun of outcome (a settlement, agreement, payment). Never a finite clause, never a gerund, never a to-infinitive: ✗ failing to reach a settlement, the case goes to trial is a dangling participle of the verb fail, not this preposition.
entries.pattern: Failing [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause], or failing that, [alternative] / [requirement], failing which [consequence]
entries.contrast: Failing and barring both introduce a condition, and both can often be swapped, but they take opposite attitudes to what they name. Failing X treats X as the outcome you wanted, and what follows is the fallback; barring X treats X as the accident that would spoil an expected result. Absent X is the legal register's version of failing X, and simple without the plain one.
entries.meaning: Names the thing that has to happen, then supplies the plan for when it doesn't. The fixed phrase failing that is by far its commonest form and is the most efficient two words in English for "if that doesn't work". 1. Introducing a fallback after a named prerequisite. 2. The fixed phrase failing that. 3. In procedural and contractual language. 4. The formula failing which. A fixed relative that hangs a consequence on the failure of what was just required. Formal, and chiefly contractual.
examples: Failing a settlement, the case goes to trial in October.
Failing agreement between the parties, the matter goes to arbitration.
Ask at the front desk; failing that, call the number posted on the door.
We'll fly out Thursday or, failing that, drive up on Friday.
Failing any objection from the floor, the motion is adopted.
Failing a qualified buyer by June, the bank takes the property.
Payment is due on the first, failing which the account goes to collections.
The tenant must cure the breach within ten days, failing which the lease terminates.

entries.ipa: /ˈɡɪv ɔr ˈteɪk/ · weak /ˈɡɪv ɚ ˈteɪk/ — the or reduces to /ɚ/ and the three words run together as one
entries.type: marginal (a frozen coordination that behaves as a preposition)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity — a number, a measure, a span of time. No gerund, no clause, and no ordinary object: ✗ give or take the traffic. It can also stand with no object at all (forty people, give or take), and in that use it is an adverb, not a preposition.
entries.pattern: [quantity], give or take [smaller quantity] / [quantity], give or take (adverb — no object)
entries.contrast: Give or take is the only member of this family that subtracts and adds at the same time: it names a margin of error on both sides of a figure, where less and minus deduct in one direction only. Against about and around, which hedge a figure without saying how far the hedge runs, give or take states the tolerance out loud. It attaches only to quantities — a figure with give or take after it is an estimate, never a count.
variants: plus or minus — the technical equivalent, at home on a spec sheet where give or take would sound careless
entries.meaning: Puts a tolerance on a number. It is the spoken American way of saying "plus or minus", and its presence is what turns a stated figure into an admitted approximation. 1. Naming a margin on a count. 2. Naming a margin on a measurement or a distance. 3. Naming a margin on time. 4. With no object — the adverb. Nothing follows, and the margin is left vague.
examples: There were sixty people in the room, give or take a dozen.
The lot holds forty cars, give or take a few.
It's about ninety miles from here, give or take five.
The ceiling is nine feet, give or take an inch.
The drive takes two hours, give or take twenty minutes.
They closed on the house in March of '09, give or take a month.
He's been at the paper thirty years, give or take.
The room seats two hundred, give or take.

entries.ipa: /ɪf ˈnɑt fɔr/ · weak /ɪf ˈnɑt fɚ/ (also written /fər/), reduced /ɪf ˈnɑʔ fɚ/ with a glottal t
entries.register: neutral to informal; the everyday American but for
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — never a gerund and never a finite clause. For a clause, write if it weren't for or if it hadn't been for, which are full clauses with their own subject and verb and not this preposition. Requires a counterfactual main clause, with would, would have, might have, or could have — exactly what but for requires.
entries.pattern: If not for [noun phrase], [subject] would (have) [verb] / [subject] would (have) [verb] if not for [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: If not for is but for in ordinary clothes: identical in meaning, identical in what it demands of the main clause, and different only in register — but for belongs to legal and formal writing, if not for to speech and general prose. Neither is except for. Except for the dessert, the meal was good reports the world as it is; if not for the dessert, the meal would have been forgettable reports a world that never happened.
variants: if it weren't for, if it hadn't been for, were it not for (formal) — clausal expansions of the same idea, and the route to take when a clause has to follow
entries.meaning: Deletes one item from the record and reports what would have followed. It is the phrase most Americans reach for when the courtroom but for would sound stiff. 1. Naming the decisive cause of a good outcome. 2. Naming the decisive obstacle. 3. In argument and explanation.
examples: If not for the neighbors, the fire would have taken the whole block.
She'd have missed the flight if not for a delay on the tarmac.
If not for the rain, we'd have finished the roof on Saturday.
If not for one bad quarter, the company would have had a record year.
The bill would have died in committee if not for two senators from farm states.
If not for the second surgery, he'd have been back at work by June.

entries.register: neutral to formal; a staple of argument and analysis
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a wh-clause (leaving aside whether it's legal, leaving aside what it costs) — never a that-clause and never a tensed clause on its own.
entries.pattern: Leaving aside [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause], leaving aside [noun phrase] / leaving aside [wh-clause] / leaving aside [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Where excluding takes an item out of a count and except for takes it out of a claim, leaving aside takes it out of the discussion: the item is not denied, only postponed, which is what lets it govern a wh-clause where most of this family cannot. Against apart from and aside from, which can be read additively, leaving aside is unambiguously subtractive. It is a true preposition here and not a dangling participle — nobody in the main clause has to be doing the leaving.
variants: setting aside, putting aside, leaving out, leaving to one side (more formal) — freely interchangeable
entries.meaning: Puts one issue to one side so that the argument can get on with the rest. It concedes that the item matters and declines, for the moment, to take it up. 1. Postponing an issue before making a point. 2. Before a wh-clause. 3. With a gerund. 4. Trailing a clause.
examples: Leaving aside the cost, the schedule alone makes it impossible.
Leaving aside the two outliers, the results are remarkably consistent.
Leaving aside whether the policy is legal, it is certainly unpopular.
Leaving aside what the repairs will run, the car is still worth keeping.
Leaving aside having to move twice, the year went about as well as we hoped.
Leaving aside paying for it, who would even run the program?
The proposal is workable, leaving aside the question of who pays for it.
Enrollment held steady all year, leaving aside a dip in the spring semester.

entries.ipa: /lɛs/ · weak /ləs/ when it sits unstressed between two figures
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an amount or a deduction — no gerund, no clause, no personal object (less him is not English).
entries.pattern: [amount] less [deduction] / [amount] less any [deduction]
entries.contrast: Less and minus both subtract, but less is the accountant's word and takes an abstract deduction (less tax, less depreciation, less attorney's fees), while minus is the arithmetic and everyday word (ten minus three, showed up minus his coat). Less is never casual and never means "without". Keep the preposition apart from the quantifier less of the fewer/less dispute (less traffic, less expensive) — that less modifies a noun or an adjective directly and has no object of its own.
entries.meaning: Subtracts one figure from another in the language of statements and settlements. It is the only word in this file that is genuinely restricted to money and measurable quantities. 1. Deducting a charge from a sum. 2. In the standing formulas of accounting. The deduction is a named line item and the whole phrase is a definition. 3. Deducting a period or a measure. Chiefly legal and surveying language. 4. Not a preposition — the quantifier and the comparative adverb. Here less modifies a noun or an adjective directly and has no object of its own; the preposition always has one.
examples: The settlement was $80,000, less attorney's fees.
She cleared the invoice amount less a two percent early-payment discount.
You'll get the deposit back less any charges for damage.
Net pay is gross salary less withholding and benefit contributions.
Revenue less cost of goods sold gives you gross profit.
Book value is original cost less accumulated depreciation.
The lease runs for one year less a day.
The parcel is a full acre less the strip taken for the easement.
The estate distributes the remaining balance less administrative expenses.
There is less traffic on the bridge after nine. (quantifier — no object)
The second bid came in less expensive by about a third. (comparative adverb)

entries.register: neutral in arithmetic and commerce; informal in the "without" sense
entries.complement: noun phrase or a number — no gerund, no clause. The word is also an adjective (a minus sign, an A minus) and a noun (that's a real minus); in those uses it has no object and is not a preposition.
entries.pattern: [number] minus [number] / [amount] minus [deduction] / minus [number] degrees / [subject] [verb] minus [thing lost]
entries.contrast: Against less, which is the formal financial word for the same operation; against without, which is the neutral and unrestricted word for absence. Informal minus meaning "without" implies loss — you turn up minus something you should have had — which is why minus his jacket works and coffee minus sugar does not.
entries.meaning: Takes one quantity away from another, and by extension takes a thing away from a person who ought to have it. The arithmetic sense is the oldest; the everyday "lacking" sense is a twentieth-century American extension and still carries a joking edge. 1. Arithmetic subtraction. 2. Below zero on a scale. 3. Commercial deduction. 4. Informally, without — implying loss. 5. Not a preposition — the adjective and the noun. No object follows either one.
examples: Nine minus four is five.
Take the total minus whatever you've already paid.
It was minus twelve at the airport this morning.
The forecast has us at minus five by Sunday night.
Your share is the sale price minus closing costs.
The refund is the ticket price minus a $35 service fee.
He came back from the trip minus a suitcase and a phone.
She showed up to the interview minus a résumé.
She got an A minus on the final. (adjective)
The commute is the one real minus of the job. (noun)

entries.ipa: /nɑt ˈkaʊntɪŋ/ · reduced /nɑʔ ˈkaʊnɪŋ/ — the t of not goes to a glottal stop before the k, and the medial nt of counting drops
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause. A what-phrase after it (not counting what the permits cost) is a fused relative, which is a noun phrase and not a clause; the test is that a plain noun can replace it (not counting the permit fees).
entries.pattern: [count or total], not counting [noun phrase] / [clause] not counting [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: The plain-speech version of excluding and exclusive of. It differs from except for in what it operates on: not counting the kids adjusts a number, while except for the kids qualifies a claim. Because it is transparently a negated participle, it can be used anywhere the arithmetic is being done out loud.
variants: not including — interchangeable and a shade more formal
entries.meaning: Corrects a total by naming what was left out of it. Nothing else in the exception family is so comfortable in speech while remaining perfectly precise. 1. Adjusting a head count. 2. Adjusting a measurement or a duration. 3. Adjusting a sum or a span.
examples: There were fourteen of us at dinner, not counting the kids.
She's read everything he wrote, not counting the early poems.
The drive takes about six hours, not counting stops.
It's a two-bedroom, not counting the office in the back.
We've spent around nine thousand, not counting what the permits cost.
He's been here twenty years, not counting the two he spent in Denver.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, adjective, adverb, prepositional phrase, gerund, or a to-infinitive (no choice other than to sue) — never a finite clause. Usually requires a negative, a question, or a totalizing word nearby, much as but does — though it is freer than but and tolerates more.
entries.pattern: [negative or question] other than [noun phrase] / [clause], other than [adjective/adverb] / no choice other than to [verb] / Other than that, [clause]
entries.contrast: Other than and except for overlap heavily, but other than insists on difference of kind, which is what lets it take an adjective or an adverb where except for cannot: other than briefly, other than legal, other than in an emergency. Do not confuse it with rather than, which expresses a choice or a preference (walk rather than drive) and never an exception.
entries.meaning: Rules out everything but the named case, or says that a thing is of a different sort from what was expected. Its stock phrase other than that is one of the most common ways an American speaker signals that a report is otherwise complete. 1. Except, apart from. 2. Before an adjective, adverb, or prepositional phrase. 3. Before a to-infinitive. 4. The discourse formula.
examples: No one other than the account holder can request a copy.
The clinic accepts no payment other than cash.
We've never used the cabin other than in the summer.
Any use other than residential requires a variance.
He had no choice other than to take the plea.
There was nothing to do other than to wait it out.
She's fine, other than a bruised shoulder.
Other than that, the week was completely uneventful.

entries.ipa: /ˌaʊtˈsaɪd ʌv/ · weak /ˌaʊtˈsaɪd əv/, reduced all the way to /ˌaʊtˈsaɪdə/ before a consonant — the of loses its /v/ exactly as it does in kind of and out of
entries.register: neutral to informal in the exception sense; chiefly American
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause. Bare outside, with no of, is also an adverb that takes no object at all (she waited outside, let's eat outside); there it is not a preposition, and the test is exactly that — the preposition has an object, the adverb has none.
entries.pattern: Outside of [noun phrase], [clause] / [negative] outside of [noun phrase] / that's outside of [noun phrase] / [verb] outside (adverb — no object)
entries.contrast: The exception sense is an Americanism; British speakers avoid it and reach for apart from. In the spatial sense, American editors trim the of — outside the building, not outside of the building — and that spatial outside is covered with the position prepositions. Against apart from and aside from, outside of is the most conversational of the three.
variants: outside — the of is optional and usually dropped in the spatial sense (outside the courthouse), but obligatory in the exception sense: Outside a few typos is not idiomatic.
entries.meaning: Puts a case beyond the reach of the statement being made — either beyond a boundary, beyond a limit of competence, or beyond the scope of a general claim. 1. Except for, apart from — chiefly American. 2. Beyond the limits or the scope of. 3. Spatially — where American editors cut the of. Correct in speech, but blue-penciled in edited prose. 4. As an adverb — not a preposition. No of, no object.
examples: Outside of a couple of late shifts, the schedule has been reasonable.
Nobody outside of the family knew he'd been sick.
Outside of Chicago, she's never lived in a big city.
That's outside of my area — you want the compliance desk.
Anything outside of routine maintenance needs written approval.
The pump is outside of warranty now.
They were standing outside of the courthouse when the verdict came down. (edit to outside the courthouse)
Park anywhere outside of the loading zone. (edit to outside the loading zone)
The dogs stayed outside all afternoon.
It's warm enough to eat outside tonight.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, a prepositional phrase, or a bare infinitive after a do-phrase (nothing to do save wait); a finite clause only through save that, which is a conjunction. Never a gerund and never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: [negative or total] save [noun phrase] / save as provided in [clause reference] (legal) / nothing to do save [bare infinitive] / save that [clause] (conjunction)
entries.contrast: Save is except in a good suit. In American prose it reads as consciously literary, and it survives most naturally in legal drafting, where save as otherwise provided is standard boilerplate. Save for is the version most writers reach for now. Do not confuse the preposition with the verb save, from which it is historically distinct — this one came in from French sauf, "except".
entries.meaning: Names the single survivor of a general negation. Almost every idiomatic use follows nothing, no one, all, or a description of emptiness, and the effect is elegiac in a way that except is not. 1. After a negative or a total. 2. In descriptions of emptiness or silence. 3. Before a bare infinitive. Only after a do-phrase, and never with to. 4. In legal drafting. The boilerplate save as otherwise provided is its last productive home. 5. Not a preposition — the conjunction save that. The preposition takes an object; save that takes a whole finite clause with its own subject and verb.
examples: All the crew were rescued save the engineer.
Nothing remained of the settlement save a chimney and a well.
He would tell them nothing save his name and the name of his ship.
The hall was dark save a single lamp at the far end.
Every window was shuttered save the one above the door.
There was nothing to do save wait for the tide to turn.
He could do nothing save watch the water come up over the sill.
The rights of the tenant are unaffected, save as provided in section 9.
All implied warranties are excluded, save as required by applicable law.
The two drafts are identical, save that the second one is dated. (conjunction — a clause follows)
He remembered nothing of the evening, save that it had rained. (conjunction)

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; a gerund is possible but uncommon. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause], save for [noun phrase] / Save for [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The current literary equivalent of except for, and the form that has largely taken over from bare save. It carries a note of bareness or desolation that except for does not: writers use it when the exception is the only thing left standing in an otherwise empty scene.
entries.meaning: Leaves one item behind after everything else has been cleared away. It is the descriptive writer's preposition, common in fiction and in longform journalism and almost absent from speech. 1. Leaving one thing standing in an empty scene. The core use, and the reason writers prefer it to except for. 2. Qualifying an otherwise clean record or an unchanged state. 3. With a gerund. Possible but uncommon, and always a little stiff.
examples: The lobby was empty save for a security guard reading a paperback.
The field was bare save for a line of fence posts along the ridge.
He owned nothing save for the clothes he was wearing.
The record is spotless save for one late filing in 2009.
The town looks the same save for the boarded-up theater on Main.
She remembers nothing of the accident save for the smell of gasoline.
The trip went perfectly, save for having to change planes twice in one day.
The house came through the winter untouched, save for losing a few shingles off the back porch.

entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause], saving [noun phrase] / saving your presence (fixed formula)
entries.contrast: The participial twin of save, and the ancestor of the legal noun saving clause — the provision that preserves something the rest of a document would otherwise wipe out. Outside legal drafting and the fossilized apology saving your presence, no living American writes it; use excepting, excluding, or except for.
entries.meaning: Preserves one item from a sweeping provision. Where save subtracts a member from a set, saving protects a right or an interest from a rule that would otherwise reach it — which is exactly the job it still does in contracts. 1. Preserving a right or a provision. 2. Preserving something from an older grant. 3. The fixed apologetic formula. Saving your presence asks pardon for what the speaker is about to say. Wholly fossilized.
examples: All previous agreements are terminated, saving the confidentiality provisions.
The judgment is affirmed, saving the appellant's right to seek further review.
The charter left the old privileges intact, saving the crown's right of appeal.
He spoke freely of the whole affair, saving the names of those involved.
Saving your presence, sir, the man is a fraud.
Saving your reverence, I never heard such nonsense in a courtroom.

entries.ipa: /ˈʃɔrt ʌv/ · weak /ˈʃɔrt əv/, reduced /ˈʃɔrɾə/ with a flapped t and no /v/ at all
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause, never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: [verb] short of [noun phrase] / Short of [verb-ing], [clause] / nothing short of [noun phrase] / be short of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Short of and barring both name a contingency, but short of names a drastic step you are declining to take, while barring names an accident you don't expect. Note also nothing short of and little short of, which are intensifiers rather than exceptions: nothing short of remarkable means "genuinely remarkable", not "except remarkable".
entries.meaning: Marks a point not reached — on a scale, on a road, or on a ladder of increasingly extreme measures. The third sense, where short is really the adjective and of the preposition, is the everyday one and shades into the others without a clean boundary. 1. Not reaching a quantity, a distance, or a standard. 2. Except by resorting to. Naming the extreme measure that has been ruled out. 3. Lacking, running low on.
examples: Donations stopped just short of the fundraising goal.
The car died a mile short of the exit.
Ticket sales came in a little short of two million.
Short of firing him, there isn't much the board can do.
Short of a miracle, that bridge won't reopen this year.
Nothing short of a subpoena will get those records released.
We're short of volunteers for Saturday.
The kitchen is two cooks short of what a Friday night needs.

entries.ipa: /wɪð ði ɪkˈsɛpʃən ʌv/ · weak /wəθ ði ɪkˈsɛpʃən əv/, reduced /wəθ ði ɪkˈsɛpʃənə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; a gerund is possible but uncommon (with the exception of having to change planes). Never a finite clause — for a clause, write except that.
entries.pattern: With the exception of [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause], with the exception of [noun phrase] / [subject], with the exception of [noun phrase], [verb agreeing with the subject]
entries.contrast: The longest word for the shortest job. Except for, apart from, aside from, other than, and bare except all subtract the same item in a third of the space, and in ordinary prose one of them is the better choice. Reach for the long form when the exception must be foregrounded, when a document has to be unmistakable about which element the exception attaches to, or when with the possible exception of is doing real hedging that no shorter phrase can do. Like everything else in this file it is a preposition, so it leaves the number of the verb alone: Every state, with the exception of Nebraska, has two chambers.
variants: with the sole exception of (emphatic), with the possible exception of (hedging) — the two standard expansions, and the reason the long form survives at all
entries.meaning: Lifts one named item out of an otherwise universal statement, slowly and on the record. The claim it modifies has to be a genuine generalization — subtracting from a statement about a single thing produces nonsense. 1. Subtracting one member from a universal claim. 2. In reports, findings, and inventories. 3. The emphatic and hedged expansions. 4. With a gerund. Grammatical, but heavy enough that except for is usually better.
examples: Every state with the exception of Nebraska has a two-chamber legislature.
With the exception of Tuesday, the entire week is booked.
The building came through the storm undamaged, with the exception of two broken windows.
All fees are refundable, with the exception of the application charge.
With the sole exception of the treasurer, no one on the board had seen the numbers.
With the possible exception of 1998, this is the wettest spring on record.
The trip went smoothly, with the exception of having to change planes in Dallas.
The renovation stayed on budget, with the exception of having to replace the wiring on the second floor.

entries.ipa: /ˈæbsənt/ — first-syllable stress, unlike the verb absent /æbˈsɛnt/ (he absented himself)
entries.complement: noun phrase, usually indefinite — a gerund is possible but rare even in legal writing, and a finite clause is impossible: write absent evidence that…, or switch to unless.
entries.pattern: Absent [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] absent [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The legal register's without or in the absence of. Against barring, which names an intervening event, absent names a missing prerequisite; against but for, which looks back at a counterfactual, absent looks forward to a condition that has not been met. British editors still flag it as an Americanism; American courts and regulators use it constantly.
entries.meaning: Declares a required thing to be missing and states what follows from its absence. It is one of the few prepositions that entered general American usage straight out of judicial opinions, and it still carries their tone. 1. Naming a missing document or authorization. 2. Naming a missing showing or proof. 3. Naming a missing condition in policy or business writing.
examples: Absent a written waiver, the filing deadline stands.
Absent an emergency, visits are limited to two hours.
Absent some showing of prejudice, the court will not disturb the verdict.
Absent any objection from the neighbors, the variance will be granted.
Absent new funding, the program shuts down in June.
Absent clear direction from the board, the staff did what seemed reasonable.

entries.ipa: /ˈfri ʌv/ · weak /ˈfri əv/, reduced /ˈfriə/ before a consonant — the of loses its /v/ as it does in kind of
entries.complement: noun phrase, usually with no determiner (free of charge, free of debt, free of liens), or a gerund (free of having to report to anyone) — never a finite clause and never a to-infinitive: ✗ free of to pay.
entries.pattern: [noun] free of [noun phrase] / [subject] is free of [noun phrase] / free of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Against without, which merely reports that a thing is missing, free of reports the absence as a benefit — whatever is missing is something you would not have wanted. That is why free of charge is idiomatic and ✗ free of a roof is not, and it is the one respect in which this preposition is not interchangeable with without, sans, or minus. Against exclusive of, which is bookkeeping for what a figure leaves out rather than a claim about anybody's good fortune.
variants: free from — the two overlap, but free of prefers a physical or financial contaminant (free of dust, free of debt) and free from prefers an oppression or a constraint (free from fear, free from interference). Devoid of is the cold formal version and is always a criticism.
entries.meaning: Reports that an unwelcome thing is missing and counts that as good news. It is the positive face of the absence family and the only member with approval built into it. 1. Free of a cost or a charge. 2. Free of a contaminant or a defect. 3. Free of an obligation or an encumbrance. 4. With a gerund.
examples: Delivery within the county is free of charge.
The account is free of monthly maintenance fees.
The lot is free of debris and ready for the foundation.
The samples came back free of any sign of contamination.
The title is free of liens and easements.
They retired free of debt for the first time in thirty years.
For one summer she was free of having to answer to anybody.
The new job leaves him free of commuting three hours a day.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ði ˈæbsəns ʌv/ · weak /ɪn ði ˈæbsəns əv/, reduced /ɪn ði ˈæbsənsə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, usually indefinite or non-count. No gerund, and never a finite clause: write in the absence of any evidence that…, or switch to the conjunction unless.
entries.pattern: In the absence of [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] in the absence of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The unfolded, fully explicit without, and the drafting register's absent. Three registers of one idea: without a permit is what a person says, absent a permit is what a court writes, in the absence of a permit is what a regulation writes. Against failing, which frames the missing thing as a prerequisite somebody was supposed to supply, in the absence of is neutral about fault. Keep the frozen preposition apart from the live phrase in The vice chair presides in the absence of the chair, where absence still means somebody is away — the same five words doing an entirely different job.
entries.meaning: States the negative condition under which the main clause holds. It is the standard opening of a default rule: this is what happens when the thing that ought to be there isn't. 1. Naming a missing document, rule, or authority. 2. Naming missing evidence or information. 3. In scientific and technical description. Here the absence is a controlled condition, not a failure.
